metadata.title: PISA Maths-Reading index and its relationship with gender and levels of performance

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Spain and applies the adjusted student weights (W_FSTUWT) for all analyses, following OECD guidance. Because PISA uses complex sampling and non-response adjustments, the authors compute standard errors and p-values using the 80 replicate weights supplied by PISA, specifically Fay’s BRR method, implemented via the R package INTSVY. The MRI is computed for each of the 10 plausible values and correlations are then averaged across plausible values, with p-values adjusted using the replicate-weight procedure. The paper does not report any additional ML-specific weighting adjustments; instead, it relies on the PISA weighting framework for the correlational analyses and for the stability of inference across plausible values.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe an explicit missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, imputation, or how missing questionnaire responses were handled) for the variables used in the correlation analyses. Given that PISA typically provides item-level missingness handling through the dataset construction process, the authors’ omission here is a reporting gap for the specific analytic variables used to compute the MRI correlations and the gender/performance subgroup analyses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the full Spanish sample included in the PISA 2018 students database (15-year-olds). The MRI is computed for all participants using mathematics and reading plausible values (10 plausible values each), and the performance-based grouping is created by running k-means clustering with 3 clusters on the maths and reading performance variables for each plausible-value pair; students are assigned to LOW/HIGH only if they fall in the same cluster across all 10 plausible-value models, otherwise they are classified as MEDIUM.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Spain (15-year-olds) Mathematics and Reading (plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (bivariate correlations; reported r and p-values, with p-values adjusted using PISA replicate weights and correlations averaged across 10 plausible values).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Spain the study leveraged Gender, Discriminating school climate, Joy/Like reading, Reading self-concept: competence, and ICT as social interaction topic to analyze the Maths-Reading Index (MRI), finding that being male and having more discriminating school climate were positively associated with MRI (maths-oriented), while Joy/Like reading and reading self-concept competence were negatively associated with MRI (reading-oriented). This indicates that gender-differentiated motivational/engagement and school-climate factors may help explain why some students polarize toward mathematics versus reading, suggesting that STEM encouragement should be tailored to both gender and reading engagement profiles, though the study is correlational and does not establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: This study conducts a secondary, non-experimental cross-sectional analysis of PISA 2018 microdata for Spain (n=35,943 15-year-olds) to build an individual Maths-Reading Index (MRI) defined as mathematics minus reading performance, computed across the 10 plausible values for each domain. The authors then examine correlations between the MRI and a wide set of contextual and educational factors, using PISA’s adjusted student weights (W_FSTUWT) and 80 replicate weights (Fay’s BRR) to obtain conservative standard errors and p-values. To refine interpretation, they create three performance-based groups (low/medium/high) using k-means clustering (k=3) on maths and reading performance for each plausible-value pair, and then analyze how correlations differ by performance level and by gender. The paper reports correlation coefficients (r) and p-values rather than predictive accuracy metrics, and it explicitly notes that correlations do not imply causality. Overall, the results suggest that gender-linked patterns and reading engagement/self-concept variables are strongly associated with students’ maths-versus-reading orientation, informing targeted STEM-support strategies.
